title: The Law of Leaky Abstractions
summary: 2002 essay stating the Law of Leaky Abstractions: every non-trivial abstraction (TCP, SQL, NFS, C++ strings, code generators) leaks, so tools save time working but not time learning, and programmers must still understand what their tools hide.

assertions.quote: Code generation tools which pretend to abstract out something, like all abstractions, leak
the only way to deal with the leaks competently is to learn about how the abstractions work and what they are abstracting
All high level tools compared to the old K&R stuff, but I still have to know the K&R stuff or I’m toast.
So the abstractions save us time working, but they don’t save us time learning.

verdicts.note: Debugging a failure inside a tool's abstraction does require understanding what it hides, but well-designed abstractions let most users avoid that learning most of the time.

Anthropic engineers self-report that delegating to Claude saves time but skips the incidental learning of doing the work manually ('skip the part where I learn how to perform a task by solving an easy instance, and then struggle to solve a more complicated instance later'), and describe a 'paradox of supervision' where checking the tool's output still requires the underlying skills; interview quotes from one company, and others in the same study report faster learning.
